Khairul Bashar (Md) and others ------ Petitioner
vs.
Collector of Customs and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: In all these Rules assessments of customs duty by the customs authority on the basis of SROs subsequent to the date of opening of Letters of Credit are under challenge. Common question of law having been involved in all these Rules these are being disposed of by this judgment. 

2. Learned Advocate for the petitioner of the respective Rule after placing the petitions and other materials on record submitted that tariff value as well as customs duty having been increased by the SROs published subsequent to the date of opening of the Letters of Credit in the respective Rule and the customs authority having claimed customs duty on the basis of subsequent SROs vested right of the respective petitioner to import goods and to pay custom duty on the basis of tariff value and custom duty prevailing at the time of opening of the letters of credit on the basis of SROs published before the date of opening of the letters of credit has been adversely affected. .Since under the impugned assessment orders customs duties have been charged on the basis of SROs issued subsequent to the date of opening of the respective letter of credit vested right of the respective petitioner has been adversely affected and such vested right cannot be taken away in view of the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Collector of Customs VS. Ahmed Hossain and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199. 

3. It appears from materials on record that under SRO No.155 dated 12-6-91 customs duty for milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening matter in powder form in retail packing of upto 2.5 Kg was 20% ad valorem and in powder form in bulk imported in bags was 40% ad volorem Under SRO No.157 dated 12-6-91 tariff value of tin packed full cream and half cream milk powder per Kg was Taka 90.00 and tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bags per metric ton was Taka 55,125.00. By SRO No: 394 dated 24-12-91 customs duty on milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening materials in powder form in retail packing  upto 2.5 Kg was increased to 25% ad valorem and in powder form in bulk imported in bags was increased to 45% ad valorem. By SRO No. ll dated 20-1-92 tariff value of full cream or half cream milk powder per Kg continued at Taka 90.00 and tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bag also continued at Taka 55,125.00 but tariff value of full cream and half cream milk in powder form imported in bags was fixed at Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton. By SRO NO.152 dated 18"6-92 tariff value of full cream and half cream milk powder packed in tin per Kg was fixed US dollars 2.50 and tariff value of full cream and half cream milk in powder form imported in bags was fixed at US dollars 1900.00 per metric ton and fat free milk powder imported in bags was fixed at US dollars 1560. Under SRO NO.152 dated 18-6-92 customs duty on milk powder packed in tin upto 2.5 Kg was 25% ad valorem and packed in bags was 45% ad valorem. Under SRO No.1 13 dated 10-6-93 rate of customs duty on milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening matter in powder form was 30%: ad valorem and in other form was 45% ad valorem. By subsequent SRO No.1 33 dated 6-7-93 customs duty on milk and cream concentrated or containing added sugar or other sweetening matter in powder form was increased to 45% ad valorem. By SRO No.214 dated 28-10-93 tariff value of milk powder imported in bulk in bags was increased to US dollars 1950.00. 

4. Petitioner of the respective writ petition claim that he is entitled to pay custom duty at the rate which was in operation on the date of opening the Letter of Credit on the basis of tariff value which was also in operation on the date of opening the letter of credit. In the aforesaid case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioner of the respective Rule it has been held that an importer acquired a vested right to- pay customs duty at the rate applicable on the date of opening of the letter of credit and he could not be charged with custom d~ at the rate imposed subsequent to the opening of the Letter of Credit. In the said decision as well as earlier decision of the Appellate Division in Abdul Hannan's case reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 interpretation of sections 19 and 30 of the Customs Act was involved. But interpretation of section 25 of the Customs Act was not involved in those decisions. Learned Advocate for the petitioner of the respective Rule contended that principle enunciated in those decisions regarding  application of the rate of customs duty will also be  applicable in respect of normal value and tariff value under section 25 of the Act. But he could not point out any decision in which it has been held that an importer is entitled to assessment of customs duty on the basis of normal value or tariff value which was in force on the date of opening of the Letter of Credit. In the case of Mostafa Kamal vs. Commissioner of Customs and others (Writ Petition Nos.4336 and 4337 of 1996) another Division Bench of this Court by judgment dated 17-12-96 considered the question as to whether an importer entitled to pay customs duty on the basis of tariff value fixed before the opening of the letter of credit or he-was to pay customs duty on the basis of tariff value which was in force on the date when the Bill of Entry was presented for assessment' of customs duty. In that decision it has been noticed that tariff value is fixed by the Government according to the suggestions of the high powered committee. In that case it has been held as follows: "since in the instant case it appears that before submission of the bill of entry before the
authority the high powered committee considered the matter and suggested for enhancement of tariff value of the goods in question at US Dollar 220 per metric ton, it  cannot be said that it was fixed arbitrarily and  the notification as well as the law itself are ultra  vires of the Constitution on the point of excessive delegation without having any  guideline. Since the notification was issued as per the decision of the high powered committee which considered the matter according to the provisions of sections 25, 30 and 30 the Customs Act, we are of the view that the impugned notification or the law itself, that is section 25(7) of the Customs Act cannot be declared ultra vires or to have been made and passed without any lawful authority." 

5. Sub-sections (1)(2) and (3) of section 25 of the Customs Act 1969 provide for determination of value of imported goods and sub-sections (4), (5) and (6) of section 25 provide for determination of value of the exported goods and sub-section (7) provides for fixation of tariff value by the Government by notification in the official .Gazette, The said- sub-section (7) is as follows: "7. Notwithstanding anything contained in this section the Government may by notification in 'the official Gazette, fix for the purpose of levying customs duties, tariff values for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty ad valorem; Provided that any imported or exported goods the declared value of which is higher than its tariff value fixed under this sub-section shall be chargeable with customs duties on the basis of its declared value. "The aforesaid provision of .sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Act provides the Government may by notification published in the official Gazette fix for the purpose of levying of custom duty, tariff value for any imported or exported goods and the said power would be exercised by the Government in spite of the provisions for determination of value of such goods under the earlier sub-sections 1-6 of section 25. But if the declared value of any such goods is higher than its tariff value then the party concerned would be liable to pay customs duty on the basis of such declared value. 

6. Normally invoice value is the basis of assessment of customs duty. To prevent under invoicing or over invoicing widely practiced by the traders either to evade payment of proper duty or to smuggle out foreign exchange power has been vested in the Government under sub-section (7) of section 25 to fix tariff value of imported or exported goods by publishing notification in the official/Gazette.  When the Government finds from materials that traders have taken resort to under invoicing to evade payment of proper customs duty it fixes tariff value of the imported goods in exercise of power under-sub-section (7) of section 25 of the Act. On the basis of change in price of goods in the foreign market from time to time Government increases or decreases the tariff value of goods to be imported in the country. This power of Government to fix tariff value by publishing notification in the official Gazette is an exceptional power which is contrary to the provisions for determination of value of the goods under-sub-sections (1)(2) and (3) of section 25. But the non-obstante provision of sub-section 7) has resolved the aforesaid contradiction between the provision of sub-sections (1), (2), (3) and the provisions of sub-section (7) of section 25. It has already been noticed from the aforesaid decision in Writ Petition Nos. B36 and 4337 of 1966 that Government revises the tariff value from time to time on the basis of recommendation of High powered Committee. Tariff value is imposed to keep the value of the imported goods in conformity with the prevailing price in the foreign countries so that importers could not in collusion with the exporters under value the goods to be imported to evade payment of proper customs duty. That being the position there is no question of importers acquiring vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value existing at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit. The aforesaid decisions of the Appellate Division relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioner having not interpreted the provisions of section 25 of the Customs Act we are not inclined to apply the principle enunciated in those decisions as to the date of the application of invoice value or tariff value. We are of the view that custom duty is payable by the importer on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice value or tariff value which was in existence at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit. But in view of the aforesaid decision of the Appellate Division Customs Authorities cannot charge customs duty on the basis of rate imposed by SRO issued subsequent to the opening of the letter or credit and an importer is entitled to pay customs duty at the rate which was in force en the date of opening of the letter of Credit. 

7. In the light of the above discussion and determination let us now consider the merit of the respective Rule. 

8. In Writ Petition No. 1032 of 1992 and Writ Petition No.1071 of 1992 petitioner of the respective writ petition was asked to declare customs duty at the rate of 25% in the Bill of Entry on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91. Letter of credit opened by the petitioner of Writ Petition No.1032 992 on 8-12-91 and by the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 1071 of 1992 on 7-12-91 when customs duty for the milk powder imported by the respective petitioner was 20% ad valorem on the basis of SRO  dated 12-6-91 So, charging customs duty at the rate  of 25%. on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91 which was issued subsequent to the opening of letters of  credit on 7-12-91 and 8-12-91 is without lawful  authority and of no legal effect So, we find merit in  these two Rules. In Writ Petition No.278 of 1992 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% on the milk powder imported by him by opening letter of credit on 14-11-91. As customs duty on the said goods on the date of opening of the letter of credit on 14-11-91 was 40%   valorem on the basis of SRO dated 12-6-91 he  was not .liable to pay customs duty at the rate of 45% imposed by SRO dated 24-12-91 issued  subsequent to the opening of the Letter of credit. Charging customs duty at the rate of 45% from the petitioner is without lawful authority and of no legal effect So we find merit in this Rule. 

9. In Writ Petition Nos. 518, 718, 785,912, 1293, 1294, 1447 and 1708 of 1992 petitioner of the  respective Writ Petition was asked by customs  authority to declare customs duty at the rate 45% and tariff value per metric ton @ Taka 65,000.00.  Petitioner of the respective Rule opened Letter of Credit on 14-11-91 when customs duty on the milk powder imported by him was @ 40% on the basis of SRO dated 12-6-91 and, as such, he was not liable to pay customs duty on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 24-12-91 @ 45%. Under SRO No.157 dated 12-6-91 tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bags was Taka 55,125.00 per metric ton but under SRO No.l1 dated 20-1-92 tariff value of fat free milk powder imported in bags per metric ton remained at Taka 55,125.00 and for the first time tariff value of full cream and half cream milk powder it imported in - bags was fixed at Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton. Petitioner having imported full cream milk powder is liable to pay customs duty @ 40% ad valorem on the tariff value of Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton on his imported full cream milk powder and he is not entitled to pay customs duty on his goods on the tariff value of Taka 55,125.00. So we find merit in these Rules in part and we hold that charging 45% customs duty instead of 40% on the petitioner is without lawful authority. But tariff value of Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton is not illegal and same is maintained for the reasons already stated. 

10. In Writ Petition No.2830 of 1992 petitioner was asked to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% and tariff value at US dollars 1900 per metric ton for the full cream milk powder imported by him in bags. He opened letter of credit on 14-11-91 and submitted Bill of Entry on 25-7-92 when tariff value was raised to US dollar 1900 by SRO dated 18-6-92 and, as such, he is to declare tariff value at the rate 1900 US dollar per metric ton. But he having opened letter of credit on 14-11-91 he was liable to pay customs duty at the rate of 40% and not 45% as demanded from him. So, we find merit in part in this Rule the charging customs duty at the rate of 45% instead of 40% from the petitioner is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. But tariff value of US dollars 1900 per metric ton is upheld. 

11. In Writ Petition No.2197 of 1992 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty @ 45% and tariff value at the rate of Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton for the milk powder imported in bags, Petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 9-3-92 when applicable rate of duty was 45% on the basis of SRO No.394 dated 24-12-91 and tariff value was Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton as per SRO. So we find no merit in this Rule which is liable to be discharged. 

12. In Writ Petition Nos.2584, 2728, 2831, 2974, 3067, 3189 and 3473 of 1992 Collector of Customs directed the petitioner of each of the Rules- to declare customs duty @ 45% and tariff value at the rate of US dollar 1900 per metric ton of full cream milk powder imported in bags. Petitioner of the respective Writ Petition opened letter of credit on 9-3-92 when applicable rate of duty was 45% on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91 and tariff value was Taka 65,000.00 per metric ton on the basis of SRO dated 20-1-92. Since customs duty was @ 45% from before the opening of the respective letter of credit petitioner of the respective Rule cannot claim to pay customs duty @ 40% on the basis of earlier SRO dated 12-6-91. In view of our opinion regarding the applicability of tariff value petitioner was liable to declare tariff value at the rate of US dollars 1900 per metric ton which was in operation on the basis of SRO dated 18-6-92 before presentation of the Bills of Entry on different dates in July, August and September, 1992. Petitioner of the respective Rule having opened letter of credit on 9-3-92 for importing full cream milk powder for which customs duty was 45% on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91 his claim that he is entitled to pay customs duty @40% on the basis of SRO No.155 dated 12-6-91 and to declare tariff value at the rate of Taka 55,125.00 per metric ton on the basis of SRO No.157 dated 12-6-91 is not tenable in view of the opinion we have already expressed. So, we find no merit in these Rules which are liable to be discharged. 
13. In Writ Petition Nos.1399, 1643, 1680, 1882 and 1883 of 1993 customs authority directed the' respective petitioner of the above writ petitions to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% on the basis of SRO No. 133 dated 6-7-93. By the said SRO customs duty was raised to 45% per metric ton on the milk powder imported packed in tins or in bags by amending the earlier SRO No.1l3 dated 10-6-93 under which customs duty was only 30% on the milk powder imported either packed in tins or in bags. Petitioner having opened letter of credit on 27-6-93 he was entitled to pay customs duty at the rate of 30% on the basis of SRO dated 10-6-93 which was in force on that date and he was not liableto pay customs duty @ 45% on the basis of' subsequent SRO dated 6-7-93. We therefore, find merit in these Rules and declare the orders in question asking the petitioner to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% under SRO dated 6-3-93 instead of SRO dated 10-6-93 to be without lawful authority customs authority directed the petitioner to declare 

14. In Writ Petition No.1321 of 1992 customs duty @25% on his imported milk powder on the basis of SRO dated 24-12-91. Petitioner opened letter or' credit on 14-12-91 for import of milk powder in packed tins of 2.5 Kg and at that time customs duty for the said goods was 20% ad valorem on the basis of SRO dated 12-6-91 and, as such, he was not liable to pay customs duty @25% on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 24-12-91. So we find merit in this Rule and as such charging on 25% customs duty on petitioner's goods instead of 20% is declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect 

15. In Writ Petition No.1931 of 1993 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty @ 45% on the basis of SRO No.133 dated 6-7-93 and tariff value per metric ton at US dollar 1950 on the basis of SRO No.214 dated 28-10-93. Petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 27-6-93 when customs duty for milk powder both packed in tins and bags was @ 30% ad valorem and, as such', he was not liable to pay customs duty @ 45% ad valorem on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 6-7-93. But he having not acquired any vested right to pay customs duty on the basis of tariff value of US dollar 1900 per metric ton as per SRO dated 18-6-92 he is not entitled to declare tariff value at US dollar 1900 per metric ton. We, therefore, find merit in part in this Rule and declare the demand of customs duty @45% instead Of 30% is without lawful authority and uphold the tariff value of US dollars 1950 per metric ton. 
16. In writ Petition No.1360 of 1993 customs authority directed the petitioner to declare customs duty @ 45%. Petitioner opened the Letter of credit on 10-6-93. By SRO dated 1O-~-93 C4stOmS duty on his imported milk powder packed in tins as well as bags was @ 30% and, as such, he was entitled to pay customs duty at that rate and not @ 45% on the basis of subsequent SRO dated 6-7-93. So, we find merit in this Rule and declare demand of customs duty @ 45% instead of 30% to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

17. In Writ Petition Nos.1365, 1366, 1516, and 1405 of 1993 petitioner of the respective writ petition was directed to declare customs duty @ 45%. Petitioner of the respective Rule opened Letter of Credit on 18-5-93,' 13-1-93 and 11-4-93 respectively when customs duty on the milk powder imported by him packed in tins of 2.5 Kg was at the rate of 25% on the basis of SRO No.151 dated 18-6-92 and, as such, petitioner of the respective Rule was entitled to pay custom duty @ 25% on the basis of the said SRO dated 18-6-92 and not liable to pay custom duty at the rate of subsequent SRO dated 6-7 -93. So we find merit in these Rules and declare the impugned orders in each of the Rules directing each of the writ petitioners to declare customs duty @ 45% instead of 25% is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

18. Petitioner of Writ Petition No.1681 of 1993 was directed by the customs authorities to declare customs duty at the rate of 45% on the full cream milk powder imported by him in retail packing of 2.5 Kg. He opened letter of credit on 10-6-93 when custom duty on his imported goods was at the rate of 30% under SRO No.113 dated 10-6-93. So demand of customs duty at the rate of 45% on the basis Of subsequent SRO No.133 dated 6-7-93 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect. So we find merit in this Rule. 

In the result, Rules on Writ Petition Nos.278, 1032, 1071 and 1321 of 1992, Writ Petition Nos. 1399, 1643, 1680, 1882, 1883, 1360, 1365, 1366, 1516, 1681 and .J405 of 1993 are made absolute, Rule in Writ Petition Nos.518, 718, 785, 912, 1293, 1294, 1447, 1708, 2830 of 1992 and Writ Petition No. 1931 of 1993 are made absolute in part and Rules in Writ Petition Nos.2197, 2584, 2728,2831,2974,3067,3189 and 3473 of 1992 are discharged.

In the facts and circumstances there will be no order to costs. Respondents are at liberty to encash the bank guarantee in full in respect of the discharged Rules and in part in respect of the Rules made absolute in part. 

End.
